pain_quote_1:
Kaazaam's G2 comment matches our experience. If you're considering working with Focusweb, read this short story so you don't get burned. If Focusweb has their own version of the conflict, I'm even ready to attach screenshots of the correspondence so you can see everything with your own eyes.

To be honest, half a year has passed already. But recently we had to completely redo the site, because it was barely usable. So I remembered all the wasted nerves and time, and I wanted to warn others so no one repeats our sad experience.

Design.
We had our own design, but they still — politely yet very persistently — kept proposing things of their own. I want to point out that a designer does their job, and a programmer does theirs. At Focusweb, the professional design ability is highly questionable, starting with elementary composition rules. And that's no surprise — programmers shouldn't be doing design. Nevertheless, the programmers kept interfering and insisting, even after we told them about 5 times that we wanted to stick to the mockup.

Deviations from the mockup.
In the end, we ended up with countless discrepancies from the mockup: alignment on the wrong side, wrong font sizes. To fix every such detail, we had to call them dozens of times. We commissioned the mockup from a professional designer so that everything would be done properly, not by eyeballing it. We paid money for that. And Focusweb butchered it all because, in their subjective opinion, it looked fine the way it was.

Revisions.
The revision stage is a very painful part. I'm afraid to misstate how long it lasted: half a year or almost a year. It looked like this:
- I make lists of about 10 items, with text describing the errors and accompanying screenshots
- the manager mostly replies with generic phrases about how she'll figure out how long it will take and let me know (something along those lines)
- from Friday to Friday I keep calling the manager, and each time I'm promised "by the end of next week"
- eventually I call Kyrylo, as the head guy, asking him to sort it out. It's hard to be angry at Kyrylo, unlike the manager who doesn't talk to clients in the best manner. Kyrylo manipulates with his politeness, since he doesn't fulfill promises on time, just like his managers.
- when, after a month or two, all the fixes are finally ready, problems appear somewhere else on the site. The cycle starts over.
- on top of everything, they regularly try to convince me that it's not the site malfunctioning but that I have browser problems. When I clear the cache, view the site on 4 other computers as well, and finally force the manager to connect to my computer via TeamViewer — that's when it turns out the problem gets solved in 20 minutes.

Mobile version.
Per our agreement, the mobile version was included in the price. They promised to adapt the mockup to device parameters. In reality, the mockup was simply cropped on the right and left in such a way that we lose 2/3 of the image. On the rest of the points, the mobile version is also practically unusable. A shame I didn't save screenshots so you could see this circus with your own eyes.

Extra payments.
For both the mobile version and many other fixes, they wanted to squeeze more money out of us. There were a few points where you could argue, but mostly it was about things we had agreed on in advance. Besides, without many of these fixes, the site simply didn't function properly.
An important point: the amounts they asked for were obviously sums no customer would ever pay. I think this shows the company simply didn't have a specialist capable of handling the assigned tasks. So Focusweb tried to frame the question so that the customer would refuse on their own.

Manager Yuliya.
I want to write about Yuliya separately — the girl who was assigned to answer all my questions. What exactly Yuliya's job consisted of, when every call I made started with Yuliya saying she doesn't handle this issue and needs to check the situation with so-and-so. It seemed to me that a manager's job is precisely to bring everyone's work together and be able to report back to the client. Forever confused, frightened, completely-not-understanding Yuliya couldn't competently answer a single one of my questions — like a secretary who was asked to watch the manager's phone during the lunch break. When I finally got the manager changed, things moved a little.

pain_quote_1:
A review of IT Academy in Dnipro, about a paid course. In August I started studying a paid HTML/CSS/JAVASCRIPT course. It cost 6,000 UAH.
A course like this could be bought on the internet for 1,500 UAH and even cheaper.

In-person lectures and daily support from the instructor were advertised. The instructor not only never provided the promised support, but also behaved unprofessionally: didn't answer the phone, cancelled scheduled meetings, scheduled meetings and then asked me to wait 40 minutes outside the door, scheduled meetings in different places and cancelled them on the same day.

The promised mentorship from the instructor never materialized, despite my numerous requests.

During the course I called the number listed on the IT Academy page in order to do something about this situation. I was told that the administrator who could discuss the situation with me simply doesn't exist, and they suggested I write a letter to HR.

After my letter to HR, the course instructor personally contacted me, and in the form of an SMS message and a letter wrote that she was ready to refund the full cost of the course, even though in my letter I had asked to refund only part of the amount for the promised support that hadn't been provided.

Nevertheless, the director of the academy informed me that refunding money is a complicated procedure and refused to reimburse it, offering instead additional hours with a different instructor.

If there had been more order and less chaos at the Academy, I would have had more trust, and I would gladly have taken the hours.

But after the wasted nerves and time, it would have been more ethical of the academy to compensate this damage with money, since the elements of the course might also turn out to be of poor quality.

If I had known there would be no support, I would have taken a course like this online for 4x less than the cost at the Academy.

I'd also like to note that the call center in Lviv often answered in a rude tone, and they didn't reach out to me for 2 weeks after I signed up for the course, which gave me reason to worry and start looking for other courses. They explained the delay by a corporate event that took place in July.

The instructor also cited the fact that she was going on a business trip to a company event in Kyiv and therefore couldn't hold the promised lesson.
